name: Paul
bio: Saul, a young man, was present at Stephen's stoning, where the witnesses laid their garments at his feet (Acts 7:58). His conversion and transformation into the apostle Paul are told in detail in the chapters ahead. Saul approved of Stephen's death and, in the great persecution that followed, ravaged the church, entering homes and dragging off men and women to prison (Acts 8:1-3). Still breathing threats against the church, Saul obtained letters authorizing him to arrest believers in Damascus, but on the road a blinding light from heaven knocked him to the ground, and he heard Jesus's voice asking why he persecuted him. Blind for three days, Saul was found by Ananias, whom the Lord had sent despite his fears, since Saul was a chosen instrument to carry Jesus's name to the Gentiles; Ananias restored his sight, and Saul was baptized and filled with the Holy Spirit. He immediately began preaching Christ in the Damascus synagogues to the astonishment of those who had known him as a persecutor, until a Jewish plot to kill him forced the disciples to lower him from the city wall in a basket. In Jerusalem, the disciples were afraid of him until Barnabas vouched for him before the apostles, after which Saul preached boldly until another plot forced him to flee to Tarsus (Acts 9:1-30). Barnabas found Saul in Tarsus and brought him to Antioch, where they taught together for a year among the growing number of Gentile believers, who were first called Christians there; when the prophet Agabus foretold a famine, Saul and Barnabas were entrusted with carrying relief to the believers in Judea (Acts 11:25-30). At Paphos on Cyprus, when the sorcerer Bar-jesus (Elymas) tried to turn the proconsul Sergius Paulus from the faith, Saul, filled with the Holy Spirit, denounced him and declared he would be struck blind, which happened at once; from this point the narrative calls him by his Roman name, Paul. In Antioch of Pisidia, Paul preached in the synagogue a lengthy sermon tracing Israel's history to David and then to Jesus as the promised Savior, raised from the dead and offering forgiveness of sins; when the Jews responded with envy and contradiction the following sabbath, Paul and Barnabas declared they would turn to the Gentiles, as the Lord had commanded, and many believed, though persecution drove them out to Iconium (Acts 13:1-52). At Lystra, Paul healed a man crippled from birth who had never walked; the crowds hailed him as the god Mercurius and Barnabas as Jupiter, moving to sacrifice to them, which Paul and Barnabas protested and barely restrained. Jews from Antioch and Iconium then stirred the crowd to stone Paul and drag him out of the city for dead, but he rose and continued on, preaching through Derbe and back through Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, appointing elders, before returning to report to the church at Antioch in Syria (Acts 14:1-28). When believers from Judea insisted that Gentiles must be circumcised to be saved, Paul and Barnabas took the dispute to the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, reporting the miracles God had worked among the Gentiles through them; the council sided with Peter and James, requiring only a few basic restrictions, and sent Paul and Barnabas back to Antioch with the decision in writing (Acts 15:1-35). Some time later, Barnabas wanted to take John Mark on a return visit to the churches, but Paul refused, since Mark had deserted them in Pamphylia; the disagreement grew so sharp that the two separated, and Paul took Silas as his new companion, departing through Syria and Cilicia (Acts 15:36-41).
